sentences.text: Romundina was a small, heavily armored acanthothoracid placoderm that inhabited shallow marine settings.
Its dermal skeleton featured star-shaped tubercles, and the skull itself was made of thin bones rich in mesodentine.
These star-shaped bumps likely served to protect the animal from predators.
This species is distinct from earlier placoderms because it lacked tesserae between the dermal bones on its skull roof.
Although Romundina clearly had a jaw, its overall cranial structure and brain proportions resembled those of jawless vertebrates.
A large, protruding bony upper lip extended forward from the nasal capsule.
The species name stellina honors the star-shaped tubercles that decorated its armor.
It likely grew a vascular spine just behind the head to deter attackers.
Tooth-like structures on its upper jaw plates showed a multi-cuspid shape, indicating they could lock together.
The first specimen of this genus was found in 1975 by the Swedish paleontologist Tor Ørvig.
The fossil came from rocks originally collected by the geologist Dr. Rómundur Thorsteinsson before being given to Ørvig.
The original find consisted mainly of a head with a complete skull roof and internal brain elements, missing most of the body.
Ørvig used a mixture of formic and acetic acid to dissolve the surrounding rock and reveal the three-dimensional specimen.
The specimen was located in a half-meter layer within a twelve-meter section of unnamed carbonate rocks at site C-8234.
Research indicates the animal mainly consumed invertebrates like crustaceans and worms using its large crushing tooth-like structures and gnathal plates.
The same geological formation holds fossils of arthrodires, heterostracans, gastropods, cephalopods, and corals.
Romundina belongs to the kingdom Animalia, the phylum Chordata, the class Placodermi, and the order Acanthothoraci.
It is characterized as occupying a middle position within the Placoderm grade.
A phylogenetic and morphological analysis by Dupret et al. (2014) suggests Romundina is related to basal members of the Arthrodira clade.
Only one species, Romundina stellina, has been described for this genus.
Romundina lived between 400 and 419 million years ago during the Early Devonian as an extinct placoderm of the family Palaeacanthaspidae in Canada.
Fossils were found near a stream in carbonate rock formations on the western side of Prince of Wales Island, suggesting a shallow water or tidal reef environment.
Associated fossils of corals and other shallow-water organisms support the idea that it lived in relatively shallow water.
During the Silurian period, Prince of Wales Island was situated close to the equator.

There is debate over whether the tooth-like structures and gnathal plates of Romundina represent the true primitive condition of Gnathostome dentition, as its disorganized dental tubercles resemble primitive features of Cyclostomes.
